title: Swapping LLMs in Under Two Seconds: A Sleep Mode for Llama.cpp
content:
Swapping LLMs in Under Two Seconds: A Sleep Mode for llama.cpp
Contents
Abstract#
Different tasks want different language models, and with a single GPU a proxy such as llama-swap has to swap them, often several times an hour. A swap between two GPU-filling models took 10.3 seconds and threw away the cached prompts of the model it replaced. One configuration change and a small wrapper, llama-sleep, which parks a model’s GPU memory in host RAM instead of stopping it, bring it down to 2.1 seconds with cached prompts intact. What remains is the copy between host RAM and GPU, held back mainly by 4 KB pages rather than by PCIe; with multi-size transparent huge pages, a kernel setting, the swap takes 1.7 seconds, about six times faster than at the start.
1 Introduction#
On my home server, a Gemma 4 12B model answers a voice assistant, and a Gemma 4 26B model handles long inputs, many of them from automations. Each fills the GPU alone, so every automation job costs two swaps: to the 26B and back.
llama-swap [1], a proxy in front of llama.cpp’s llama-server [2], does the swapping: it stops the running model and starts the requested one. That costs a full model load, and the voice model loses its cached system prompt of about 8,000 tokens; recomputing it delayed the first spoken word by another 6–7 seconds.
vLLM has a sleep mode for this [3], and llama-swap ships a vllm-wrapper that uses it [4, 5]. llama-server’s --sleep-idle-seconds unloads a model after idle time [6], but it frees the KV cache with it and reloads the weights on the next request.
The question of this note: how fast can a swap behind llama-swap get, with llama-swap unchanged and as little extra software as possible?
2 Setup and method#
- Hardware: NVIDIA RTX 3060 12 GB on PCIe 3.0 x16 (the Ryzen 5 PRO 5650G limits the slot to gen 3), 125 GB DDR4, Fedora 44, driver 615.71.
- Software: llama-swap v263 and llama.cpp b11552 (CUDA 13) in one container (ghcr.io/mostlygeek/llama-swap:v263-cuda13-b11552-non-root). All model files are in the page cache.
- Models: Gemma 4 12B QAT and Gemma 4 26B A4B QAT, both UD-Q4_K_XL. The 12B uses 7.9 GiB of GPU memory, the 26B 11.1–11.3 GiB with part of its expert weights on the CPU. For a worst case, two separate 26B processes are swapped against each other.
- Metric: time from sending a request for the other model until its first token arrives (max_tokens 1), measured at the client. Each value is the mean of two steady-state rounds of the cycle 26B → 26B → 12B.
- Breakdowns: llama-swap logged with microsecond timestamps and the wrapper logged every step; client, proxy and wrapper events were merged into one timeline.
3 Where the ten seconds go#
A baseline swap between the two 26B models takes 10.3 seconds: stopping the old process, starting the new one, loading the weights and waiting until llama-swap’s health check succeeds. Two parts of that are pure overhead.
- Probing memory. llama.cpp’s --fit finds out how many layers fit on the GPU by creating trial contexts, again at every start. A fixed split (--n-cpu-moe 14 for the 26B) halves the swap to 5.5 seconds. The catch: the split is tuned by hand for one model on one GPU. llama-sleep’s wake does not depend on it, but every cold start does.
- Polling. llama-swap checks the new model’s health 250 ms after starting it and then once a second [1], so a model that is ready just after a check waits up to a second.
Skipping llama.cpp’s warmup run (--no-warmup) changes nothing measurable. What remains is loading weights that the machine already holds in RAM, and that is what parking avoids.
4 Parking instead of stopping#
4.1 What cuda-checkpoint can do#
Since driver 550, NVIDIA’s cuda-checkpoint tool can suspend the CUDA state of a running process [7]. It copies the process’s device memory into host memory and frees the GPU; a second call copies it back to the same addresses.
On the running 12B this took 3.8 seconds out and 1.5 seconds back in, and the model answered correctly afterwards.
Two observations shaped the design:
- A request to a parked model crashed it. A suspended llama-server still answers /health with 200, so llama-swap considers it ready and forwards the request while the restore is still running. The process then segfaulted inside libcuda. NVIDIA’s documentation says such calls may block until CUDA is resumed [7]; with llama-server they did not.
- A frozen process cannot be woken. Freezing the container would keep requests away, but the restore then hangs: it runs on a CUDA restore thread of the target process (cuda-checkpoint --get-restore-tid reports its ID) [7, 8], and the cgroup freezer stops that thread too.
4.2 llama-sleep#
llama-sleep [9], MIT-licensed, follows the pattern of llama-swap’s vllm-wrapper [4]: a small program that is the model’s cmd and cmdStop. Figure 1 shows how it swaps two models.
macros:
  "serve": llama-sleep serve --name ${MODEL_ID} --listen 127.0.0.1:${PORT} --idle 5s --
  "sleep": llama-sleep sleep --name ${MODEL_ID} --stop-pid ${PID}
models:
  "gemma-26b": { cmd: "${serve} llama-server ...", cmdStop: "${sleep}" }
- It holds requests. llama-server runs as a detached daemon that only llama-sleep can reach, through a Unix socket or an internal container port. llama-sleep is the reverse proxy on llama-swap’s port and holds every request, the health check included, until the model is awake and healthy. This prevents the crashes and replaces llama-swap’s polling: the health check returns the moment the model is ready.
- It parks in the background. With --idle 5s, a model that has been idle for five seconds is parked while nobody waits. A later swap then only has to wake the new model.
- It wakes on start. llama-swap starts serve because a request is waiting, so the wake begins at once instead of at the first health check.
- It is one file. llama-sleep is a single Go binary of about 7 MB, built without cgo. It calls the checkpoint functions of the CUDA driver API (cuCheckpointProcess*) [7, 8] through dlopen [10] and needs neither cuda-checkpoint nor the CUDA toolkit.
- It fails safe. A changed command line replaces a parked daemon instead of resuming it; a failed restore or a crashed daemon ends serve, so llama-swap notices and starts the model fresh on the next request.
5 Results#
The steps are cumulative: the fixed layer split from section 3; holding requests, parking in the background and waking on start from section 4.2; and huge pages from section 6. Each removes a visible part of the swap, and parking brings the largest gain (Figures 2 and 3). The direction not shown, from the 12B to the 26B, behaves like the 26B pair: 10.1 seconds at the start, 1.6 at the end.
Cached prompts survive. A 9,589-token prompt sent to the 12B again after a swap to the 26B and back was answered with one token processed and 9,588 taken from the cache; after a cold start, all 9,589 had to be processed.
Parking pays off only in the background. Parked during a swap, the slower copy direction sits on the critical path: with the fixed split, 26B → 12B then takes 6.8 seconds against 3.5 seconds for stopping the old model.
With parking in the background and the wake on start, everything around the copy shrinks to 82 ms: llama-swap, process start, unlock, health check, prompt and first token. The other 1,784 ms are the copy back to the GPU (Figure 4).
6 The copy: page faults, not the bus#
Both copies, out of the GPU when parking and back in when waking, are far slower than the link. A small benchmark with the CUDA driver API (1 GiB copies, best of five) shows what the link can do: 13.4 GB/s from pinned host memory to the GPU and 13.2 GB/s back, and about 12–13 GB/s with ordinary memory that has been touched before. Copied from the GPU into a freshly allocated buffer, the same data moves at only 2.2 GB/s, which is exactly llama-sleep’s park speed. report.summary: llama-sleep parks a llama.cpp model's GPU memory in host RAM, letting a single GPU swap LLMs in 1.7–2.1 seconds with cached prompts intact instead of 10.3.
report.background: Local LLM setups increasingly run several specialized models rather than one: a small model for a low-latency voice assistant, a larger one for long automation jobs. On a single GPU each model fills memory alone, so a proxy such as llama-swap must stop one process and start another for every switch — potentially several times an hour. That is a full model reload plus, crucially, the loss of cached system prompts; the author's 8,000-token voice prompt cost another 6–7 seconds to recompute, wrecking first-word latency. vLLM already ships a sleep mode, and llama-swap has a wrapper for it, but llama.cpp's own --sleep-idle-seconds unloads the KV cache along with the weights. Since NVIDIA driver 550, however, the driver's checkpoint API can suspend a whole CUDA process — device memory out to host RAM, then back to the same addresses — which is the primitive this work exploits.
key_points: Parking beats stopping: instead of killing a model, llama-sleep calls the CUDA driver's checkpoint functions to copy its GPU memory into host RAM and free the device, then restores it in place on the next request. On the 12B model that took 3.8 seconds out and 1.5 seconds back, and the model answered correctly afterwards.

The wrapper holds requests. A suspended llama-server still answers /health with 200, so llama-swap would forward traffic mid-restore and segfault it. llama-sleep becomes the reverse proxy on llama-swap's port, queuing every request — health checks included — until the model is awake, and the health check returns instantly instead of on a 1-second poll.

Wins are cumulative. Tuning llama.cpp's memory probing into a fixed layer split (--n-cpu-moe 14) halves a swap to 5.5 seconds; background parking plus wake-on-start brings it to 2.1; enabling multi-size transparent huge pages lands at 1.7 seconds, about six times faster than the 10.3-second baseline. The reverse direction goes from 10.1 to 1.6 seconds.

Cached prompts survive swaps. A 9,589-token prompt re-sent to the 12B after a round trip to the 26B was answered with one token processed and 9,588 pulled from cache; after a cold start all 9,589 had to be recomputed. This is the difference between a snappy voice assistant and a six-second pause.

The bottleneck is page faults, not PCIe. Pinned-memory copies hit 13.4 GB/s each way, but copying into the freshly allocated buffer the driver creates during parking runs at 2.2 GB/s, because every 4 KB page must be faulted in and zeroed. Of the final 1,866 ms, only 82 ms is everything besides the copy back to the GPU.
report.impact: For the AI industry this narrows a real feature gap: vLLM has had sleep mode, llama.cpp has not, and this shows the missing piece is a wrapper around an existing driver API rather than deep engine surgery. It makes single-GPU multi-model serving — routing each task to the model that suits it — genuinely practical on consumer hardware, and it points at a broader lever: huge pages and allocation strategy matter as much as the bus. Developers get a ~7 MB MIT-licensed Go binary that drops into a llama-swap config, plus a reusable pattern: hold requests at the proxy, park in the background, wake at start. Caveats remain — pinned host RAM must be large enough to hold a whole model, the 1.7 s figure needs a kernel setting, the fixed layer split is hand-tuned per model and GPU, and the cgroup freezer must be avoided. Users see a faster local assistant with much less repeated prompt processing.
report.tools: llama-swap is the proxy to configure; llama-sleep is the MIT wrapper to try, plugged in as cmd/cmdStop. Watch llama.cpp's llama-server flags (--n-cpu-moe, --fit, --no-warmup, --sleep-idle-seconds) and NVIDIA's cuda-checkpoint tool / cuCheckpointProcess* driver API. For comparison, see vLLM's sleep mode and llama-swap's vllm-wrapper. The transparent-hugepage kernel setting (multi-size THP) is worth enabling if you measure swap times yourself.
